newsitem.title: CANADA: New Canada lumber quotas give companies less.
newsitem.headline: New Canada lumber quotas give companies less.

text.p: The Canadian government said on Monday that it has set new softwood lumber allocations for the second year of a trade agreement between Canada and the United States.

Almost everyone will get a bit less quota this year compared to last year, said Gordon Chestnut, administrator of the softwood lumber section at the Department of Foreign Affairs. He said the new numbers were sent out late Friday to more than 500 mills across Canada.
"Everybody for the most part likely goes down a little bit," Chestnut said.

He said the reason for the change is that last year's bonus quota space was split up and given out to new companies and to companies suffering hardship. But this year, the bonus quota becomes a permanent regular quota for those new and "hardship" companies, he said.
"Those numbers were all squeezed back in to the 14.7 million board feet allocation for year two," Chestnut explained.

The five-year quota agreement limits fee-free exports from Canada's top four exporting provinces to 14.7 million board feet of lumber per year. Companies exceeding their quotas must pay a fee ranging from US$50 to US$100 per 1,000 board feet.
Bonus quota is earned if lumber prices are higher than expected.
Traders said the new numbers had not yet trickled into the market and therefore had not yet had much an effect. The market has been nervously awaiting the new quota.
Mills in eastern Canada, especially Quebec, have complained that the quota system favored mills in Alberta and British Columbia while penalizing expanding mills in the east.
Eastern Canadian mills hope to see an improved balance with the new quotas for the second year, said broker Gilbert Garant with Whalen Beliveau and Associates in Montreal.
"That's what we're hoping for," he told Reuters.
But companies would be wrong to expect any radical changes in the distribution of the quota, Chestnut said.
"In general, everybody's will go down," he said, adding that on average the decline for most mills will be minimal, about 0.1 percent.

"There were some companies that did go up, because Ontario and B.C. did some readjusting as far as the formulas used for the adjustments," Chestnut noted. "There were some adjustments in Quebec as well."
Provincial authorities were in charge of the changes.
Chestnut said the second year of the five-year agreement should lead to a smoother lumber market, compared to last year's nervous and volatile market.
Last year, lumber prices were volatile at the end of each quarter as mills rushed to fill their quotas and avoid losing their allocations.
With firm allocations this year similar crushes are unlikely. "Now we're into one system, so we don't need to be worried about first-come first-served any longer," Chestnut said.
Companies can carry over their unused quarterly quota space from quarter to quarter, but they cannot carry unused quota into another year, he explained.
((Heather Scoffield, Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613 235-6745))
